10.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this hip prosthesis?"
- "**Hemiarthroplasty** replaces the femoral head; **total hip arthroplasty (THA)** also replaces the acetabulum."
- "**Unipolar** moves on the patient's acetabulum; **bipolar** adds an inner head in a mobile shell."

- Arthroplasty types: **resection**, **interposition**, **mould**, **replacement** (Nagah)

| Implant (Handbook) | Look for | Moves at |
|---|---|---|
| **Austin Moore** | one piece, **fenestrated** stem, collar | native acetabulum |
| **Thompson** | one piece, **solid** stem, collar | native acetabulum |
| Modular unipolar | stem + large head on taper | native acetabulum |
| **Bipolar** | inner head locked in shell | inside shell + on acetabulum |
| **THA** | stem, head, liner, cup | head on liner |
| **Dual mobility** (tripolar) | polyethylene (PE) ball, polished shell | two areas, one centre |
| **Resurfacing** | metal cap with peg, metal cup | metal on metal |

- Resurfacing suits men with large heads, **56–64 mm**; the **Birmingham** survives (Prof Khaled Fawzy)
- Resurfacing fails by **neck fracture**: small necks, women, notched neck

- Austin Moore and Thompson prostheses
- Cemented bipolar hemiarthroplasty at 75 years
- THA parts: shell, liner, head, stem
- Resurfacing implant, and resurfacing on X-ray

10.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this?" (a Thompson)
- "A **Thompson**: one-piece, unipolar, **cemented** hemiarthroplasty with a solid stem."
- "Its look-alike, the **Austin Moore**, is uncemented; bone grows through its **windows**."

### Austin Moore vs Thompson
| (Nagah; Handbook) | Austin Moore | Thompson |
|---|---|---|
| Stem | holes: extraction, bone healing | solid, no holes |
| Fixation | press-fit, no cement | cemented |
| Calcar | must be intact | cement copes with fracture |
| Lateral shoulder | squared, with extraction hole | rounded |

- Both are one piece: leg length and tension are fixed at insertion
- Cemented stems give better function and less thigh pain
- Both are now kept for **very limited mobility**

PITFALL — "which one has the shoulder?"
- Nagah gives the shoulder to the Thompson; the photos show it on the **Austin Moore**
- Say → "**Austin Moore: windows and a square shoulder. Thompson: solid, rounded, cemented.**"

- Failed Austin Moore: fenestrated stem, acetabular erosion
- Bilateral cemented Thompson hemiarthroplasties

### Insertion — Thompson
1) Approach: **lateral** (fewer dislocations) or posterior
2) Head size: template on a true-size or **magnification**-corrected X-ray
3) Cut the neck; clear the hard lateral neck so the calcar does not split
4) Ream, cement, insert the stem; reduce gently → no shaft fracture

### Bipolar
- Inner head in a PE-lined shell, shell on acetabulum → wider safe range of motion (ROM)
- Many bipolars stop moving inside and act as **unipolar**
- A **22-mm** inner head moves mainly inside; a 32-mm mainly outside (Rockwood)

- Unipolar vs bipolar: no difference in dislocation, infection or reoperation
- A dislocated bipolar may **dissociate** on closed reduction → open reduction
- Safe at **75**; at 60–70 it may erode the acetabulum (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- THA instead: independently mobile, no cognitive impairment, acetabular disease

- Cementless bipolar: arrows on inner and outer heads
- Uncemented modular hemiarthroplasty in good position

10.03.t: 10.3 THA Components — Stem, Head, Liner, Cup
10.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "name the parts of this total hip"
- "**Stem**, **modular head** on the **trunnion**, **liner**, porous metal **shell**."
- "Stem always metal; head always hard — cobalt-chrome (CoCr) or ceramic, never PE (Handbook)."

### The taper (trunnion)
- The trunnion is a **Morse taper**; commonest size **12/14 mm**
- Tapers differ between makers: never mix them → dissociation, corrosion
- A long neck on a head ≤ 32 mm has a **skirt**

- Modular heads, metal and ceramic, on stem tapers
- Femoral heads: stainless steel, oxidised zirconium, CoCr

### Materials — which part, which metal
| Material (Prof Mahmoud Fahmy) | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **CoCr** | heads, cemented stems | low wear, stiffest metal |
| **Stainless steel** | cemented stems | stiff, spares the cement |
| **Titanium** | cementless stems and shells | near-bone modulus; poor wear, no bearing |
| **Tantalum** | porous cups, augments | very porous, low modulus |

- Stiffness: ceramic > CoCr > stainless steel > titanium > bone > polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) > PE

### Modularity — what goes wrong
- Micromotion at the head–neck junction → **fretting corrosion**
- **Trunnionosis**: the head spot-welds onto the trunnion

- Retrieved head bore and trunnion with corrosion

10.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which bearing is this?"
- "Hard-on-soft: head on PE. Hard-on-hard: ceramic-on-ceramic (CoC) or metal-on-metal (MoM)."
- "**Metal-on-PE** is the gold standard; **highly cross-linked PE (HXLPE)** cut wear **80–90%** (Campbell)."

- Joint force: **3×** body weight walking, 5.5× up stairs (Prof Khaled Fawzy)

| Bearing (Prof Mahmoud Fahmy) | Wear, µm/year | Plus | Minus |
|---|---|---|---|
| CoCr on PE | **120–200** | cheap, forgiving, easy revision | particles → osteolysis |
| Ceramic on PE | 80–120 | half the wear | ceramic cost |
| CoCr on HXLPE | 0–25 | large heads | lower fatigue strength |
| MoM | 1–5 | largest head, stable | ions, pseudotumour |
| CoC | **< 1** | least wear, inert particles | fracture, squeaking, unforgiving |

- Bearings side by side, from CoC to metal-on-PE
- Metal-on-PE, ceramic-on-PE and CoC on one X-ray

### Polyethylene
- Radiation in vacuum or inert gas **cross-links** PE; in air it oxidises
- HXLPE gets **5–10 Mrad**, then one of two heat steps (Campbell)

| After radiation (Campbell) | Result |
|---|---|
| **Remelting** above melting point, ≈ 135 °C | no free radicals, weaker |
| **Annealing** | stronger, radicals remain |

- A 32-mm head gives ≈ **8°** more ROM than a 28-mm (Campbell)
- PE forgives impingement and a steep cup; metal and ceramic fail catastrophically
- Wear particles → macrophages → cytokines → osteoclasts → **osteolysis**
- A head off-centre in the cup = **PE wear**

- Retrieved HXLPE liner with rim impingement damage

### Ceramic
- Today's ceramic: **BIOLOX delta**, alumina with zirconia, coloured **pink**
- Delta fracture ≈ **1 in 100,000**; pure alumina 1 in 5,000 (Campbell)
- Fracture risk: **small heads**, **short necks**, cup **retroversion**
- Ceramic wets better: contact angle **45°** vs 86° on metal (Prof Khaled Fawzy)

- A fractured ceramic is often **invisible** on X-ray → CT, revise **at once**
- "**Once a ceramic, always a ceramic**": particles stay, so revise to ceramic (Prof Mahmoud Fahmy)
- Intact taper → **metal-sleeved** ceramic head; damaged taper → new stem

- BIOLOX generations, 1974 to delta 2003
- Fractured ceramic head, retrieved in pieces
- Stripe wear on ceramic head and liner

### Metal-on-metal
- Metal ions → **pseudotumour**, **ALVAL** (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion)
- Avoid in **renal impairment** and women of childbearing age
- Painful MoM, normal X-ray → blood cobalt, chromium and **MARS** MRI (metal artifact reduction sequence)

- Pseudotumour around MoM hip on MARS MRI

### Dual mobility
- Large PE ball in a **polished** shell → stable without a constrained liner's ROM loss
- Its own risk: **intraprosthetic dislocation**
- It is a **total** hip, not a bipolar: the shell sits in the acetabulum

- Dual mobility cup: PE ball inside polished shell
- Dual mobility cups on X-ray at 5–6 years

### Choosing by age
| Age | Bearing (Prof Khaled Fawzy) |
|---|---|
| < 60, active | CoC, head 32 or 36 mm |
| 60–65 | CoC or ceramic on HXLPE |
| 65–75 | ceramic on HXLPE |
| > 75 | CoCr on HXLPE |

PITFALL — "CoC for every young patient?"
- Prof Khaled Fawzy: CoC below 60; Prof Sherif Khaled: hard-on-soft only
- Say → "**Under 60 CoC or ceramic-on-HXLPE; hard-on-soft if the team is not set for CoC.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Head hard, liner soft, cross-link the PE, keep the ceramic pink**

10.05.t: 10.5 Cemented Stems — Composite Beam vs Loaded Taper
10.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what kind of cemented stem is this?"
- "**Composite beam**: rough, collared, must not move. **Loaded taper**: polished, collarless, subsides."
- "Cement is a **grout, not a glue**: it fills and interlocks, it does not stick."

| (Prof Ahmed Hazem) | Composite beam (shape-closed) | Loaded taper (force-closed, taper-slip) |
|---|---|---|
| Surface | rough, matte | **polished** |
| Shape | anatomic | straight, tapered in **two planes** |
| Collar | wanted, loads calcar | harmful, blocks subsidence |
| Tip | no void | **void**, hollow centraliser |
| Stability | initial; any movement fails | secondary; subsides in year 1 |
| Forgiving | no | yes |

- Subsidence compresses the cement → **hoop stress** in bone, like barrel hoops
- Loaded-taper examples: **Exeter**, collarless polished taper (**CPT**)
- Never mix the two concepts in one stem

- Cemented femoral stems, side by side
- Loaded taper (A) and collared composite beam (B) on X-ray

### Design numbers
- The stem fills ≈ **80%** of the canal
- Mantle: ≈ **4 mm** proximal, 2 mm distal (Campbell)
- Over **75**, registries favour cemented stems: fewer periprosthetic fractures

- Loaded taper stem with void below the tip
- Fractured cemented polished stem, retrieved

### When cemented
- Cement for elderly, irradiated, deformed or **Dorr C** femora; Dorr **A–B**, young → cementless
- Cemented THA survives **97%** at 10 years, 89% at 15 (Prof Sherif Khaled)

- Dorr A, B and C proximal femurs on X-ray

10.06.t: 10.6 Cementless Stems — Where Does It Grip?
10.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this cementless stem?"
- "Press-fit first; then bone grows **into** a porous coating or **onto** a blasted surface."
- "I name it by where it grips: **Khanuja** types 1–6."

| Type (Prof Ahmed Hazem) | Shape | Grips |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | single wedge, thin laterally | metaphysis |
| 2 | double wedge, **fills the metaphysis** | metaphysis |
| 3A | tapered, **round** (conical) | metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction |
| 3B | tapered, **splined** (Wagner) | proximal diaphysis |
| 3C | tapered **rectangular**, fully coated | junction; four-point hold |
| 4 | **cylindrical, fully coated** | diaphysis, scratch fit |
| 5 | **modular** body + distal stem | each part separately |
| 6 | **anatomic**, left and right | metaphysis |

- Type 3 leads the market; type 4 cracks the diaphysis and is declining

- Khanuja cementless stem types 1–6
- Type 1 and type 2 stems
- Type 3A, 3B and 3C stems
- Type 4 fully coated and type 6 anatomic stems

### Surfaces
- Ingrowth: **sintered beads**, titanium **fibre mesh**, **plasma-sprayed** titanium, **porous tantalum**
- Ongrowth: **grit-blasted**; weaker, so it needs a double-wedge press-fit
- Bone needs pores of **50–400 µm** and minimal micromotion (Prof Mahmoud Fahmy)
- **Hydroxyapatite (HA)** is an osteoconductive coating → less migration

- Ingrowth: beads, fibre mesh, tantalum; ongrowth: grit-blast, plasma titanium, HA
- Hydroxyapatite-coated stems: Corail and collared Actis

### Short stems and fit
- A **short stem** is about half the **14-cm** standard; it grips the metaphysis only
- Extensive coating → **proximal stress shielding** and distal **spot welds**

- Short stem beside a standard stem on X-ray
- Spot welds, stress shielding, pedestal on X-ray

10.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this cup?"
- "Cemented cup: **all-PE**, grooves, spacers, **wire marker**."
- "Cementless cup: **porous titanium shell**, press-fit, ± screws, modular liner — the default."
- "Cement fails in **shear** at the socket."

| | Cemented cup | Cementless shell |
|---|---|---|
| Look for | white PE, grooves, spacers, flange | porous dome, screw holes, liner |
| On X-ray | lucent; **wire marker** shows position, wear | dense shell, screws |
| Fixation | **2–4 mm** mantle | press-fit, under-ream **1–2 mm** |
| Best for | old, low demand, poor bone | almost everyone else |

- Cemented cup: spacers, grooves, flange, wire
- Charnley UHMWPE cup with radiographic wire marker

### Cementless shell
- **Dual-radius** cups are obsolete: they can fracture the acetabulum
- Cementless cup survives **96%** at 10 years, ≈ 90% at 20 (Prof Fady Kamal)
- Line-to-line reaming gives no intrinsic stability → screws, spikes or fins

- Cementless cups, first to third generation
- Shell with screw holes and PE liner

### Liners
- Shapes: **neutral**, **lipped**, **offset**, **anteverted**
- **Constrained**: a locking ring or captured inner bipolar holds the head
- Use it for weak abductors, neuromuscular disease, or recurrent dislocation with **well-placed** parts (Campbell)
- Malposition > **10°** → revise that part, not a constrained liner (Prof Ahmad Azzam)

- Liner shapes: neutral, lipped, offset
- Constrained liners: tripolar design and peripheral locking ring

### Screws — the quadrants
- Line from the anterior superior iliac spine (**ASIS**) through the cup centre, plus a perpendicular

| Quadrant (Campbell) | Screws |
|---|---|
| **Posterosuperior** | safest |
| **Anterosuperior** ("death zone") | external iliac vessels |
| **Anteroinferior** | obturator nerve and vessels |

- Acetabular quadrants for safe screw placement
- Porous metal augment filling a rim defect

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Posterosuperior is the safe seat; anterosuperior is the death zone**

10.08.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is in this packet?"
- "**Powder**: PMMA polymer, benzoyl peroxide initiator, barium sulphate or zirconia opacifier, ± antibiotic."
- "**Liquid**: methyl methacrylate monomer, dimethyl-p-toluidine accelerator, hydroquinone stabiliser."

- Setting is exothermic: **80–85 °C** in vitro, much lower in the body
- Strong in compression, poor in tension; brittle and **notch-sensitive**

- Cement packet: powder sachet and liquid monomer ampoule

### Phases
| Phase | Lasts until |
|---|---|
| **Dough time** | no longer sticky to gloves |
| **Working time** | cement is hard |
| **Setting time** | dough + working time |

- Inject at early dough, ≈ **4 min**; insert the stem at medium dough, ≈ 6 min (Simplex)

### Cementing generations
| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd (modern) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Canal | no restrictor, no wash | **restrictor**, brush | **pulsatile lavage**, dry |
| Mixing | by hand | hand or instrument | **vacuum** or centrifuge |
| Delivery | finger packing | **gun**, retrograde | gun + **pressuriser** |
| Centralisers | distal only | proximal + distal | proximal + distal |

- The restrictor sits **1–2 cm** below the stem tip

| Barrack grade (Prof Mahmoud Fahmy) | Mantle |
|---|---|
| A | white-out |
| B | lucency ≤ 50% |
| C | lucency 50–99% |
| D | 100%, or no cement below tip |

- Cement gun with femoral pressuriser, canal restrictor, cup pressuriser
- Cemented stem and cup, well-filled mantle

- The antibiotic is a **heat-stable**, **water-soluble** powder; two drugs elute better
- Keep the dose under **10%** of the cement weight (Prof Mohamed Abdel Moneim)
- Spacer cement is **hand-mixed** → more pores, more elution

10.09.t: 10.9 Instruments — In the Order You Use Them
10.09.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this hemispherical cutter?"
- "An **acetabular reamer**: start small and go up in 1–2 mm steps."
- "Ream to — not through — the medial wall, to a bleeding hemisphere."

1) **Acetabular reamers**: start below the planned size
2) **Trial cup** checks fit and coverage; then the **cup impactor** with its alignment guide
3) Screws: flexible drill and **depth gauge**

4) **Box osteotome** opens the canal; ream **lateral** → no varus
5) **Broaches** (rasps): start ≥ **2 sizes** smaller; rotate for anteversion
6) **Trial neck and head**: check length, offset, stability
7) **Stem inserter**; then the head on a **clean, dry taper**, one blow

- Acetabular reamer, then shell on its impactor
- THA instrument trays and the canal finder

10.10.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this long fluted stem?"
- "A **modular tapered fluted** (Wagner) revision stem: conical for any version, **splines** for rotation."

### Femur
- A long stem must pass the lowest screw hole by **two cortical diameters**

- Splined tapered revision stem and its X-ray
- Modular revision stems: bodies and distal parts

### Acetabulum
- Cavitary loss → **impaction grafting**; a **Müller ring** protects the graft
- Segmental loss → structural graft or **augment**
- Big loss or discontinuity → reconstruction ring or **cup-cage**

- Reconstruction cage with flanges on a pelvis model
- Mesh, screws and ring after impaction grafting

### Antibiotic spacers
- **Static** (cement block) or **articulating**: PROSTALAC, preformed, hand-moulded
- PROSTALAC = prosthesis of antibiotic-loaded acrylic cement; loose, easy to remove
- Elutes for **4–6 weeks**; leave it 2–3 months at most

- Spacers: PROSTALAC, ready-made, custom-made
- Preformed antibiotic hip spacer

### Tumour
- **Megaprosthesis**: modular segments replace the proximal femur

- Proximal femoral replacement: modular segments and X-ray

10.11.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is this hip loose?"
- "**Gruen 1–7** round the stem, **DeLee–Charnley I–III** round the cup; then lines, migration, broken metal."

- Gruen: **1** lateral top, **4** tip, **7** medial calcar; lateral view 8–14
- DeLee–Charnley: **I** superior, **II** middle, **III** inferior third of the cup

- Gruen zones and Charnley acetabular zones

| Component | Loose when (Prof Sherif Khaled) |
|---|---|
| Cemented stem | broken stem or cement, stem moved |
| Cementless stem | progressive lines, **subsidence**, **pedestal** |
| Cup | migration > **2–5 mm**, inclination change |

- A loaded taper subsiding **1–2 mm** in year 1 is normal
- A cemented stem breaks by **cantilever** bending: tip fixed, top loose

- Pedestal and subsidence, unstable cementless stem
- Broken cemented stem, fixed distally

- Septic: periostitis, endosteal scalloping, lucency growing week by week

- Eccentric head in the cup at 7 years
- Cup inclination change at 4 years = loose

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Seven round the stem, three round the cup; lines, sinking, breaking, moving**
